verses.translation: And after{H310} this I heard{H8085} one voice{H6963} from a great{H1419} company saying: HalleluYah! And glory{H3519} and might{H1369} and splendor{H8597} shall be to YHWH{H3068} our Lord{H113}.

one_way_hebrew: HalleluYah (הַלְלוּיָהּ) is organically HEBREW — it means 'Praise Yah!' and embeds the divine name. Greek Ἁλληλούϊα is a transliteration of the Hebrew. The fact that the Greek must BORROW the Hebrew word demonstrates Hebrew priority for this liturgical formula.

Uses כָבוֹד וּגְבוּרָה וְתִפְאֶרֶת (kavod ugvurah vetiferet — 'glory and might and splendor') — THREE praise attributes. Greek has FOUR: σωτηρία καὶ δόξα καὶ τιμὴ καὶ δύναμις ('salvation and glory and honor and power'). The Hebrew triad kavod/gevurah/tiferet parallels 1 Chronicles 29:11 — 'Yours, O YHWH, is the greatness and the might (הגבורה) and the splendor (התפארת) and the glory (ההוד) and the majesty.' A back-translator from Greek's four terms would not independently arrive at the Chronicles formula.
Uses חַבְרוּתָה (chavrutah — 'company/fellowship') — the same rabbinic term as ch. 17:15. Greek: ὄχλου πολλοῦ ('great multitude').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: three praise terms (glory, might, splendor). Greek: four terms (salvation, glory, honor, power). Greek adds 'salvation' and 'honor.'
Hebrew: 'to YHWH our Lord.' Greek: 'to the Lord our God.' Different divine title.
Greek adds 'in heaven' (ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ) — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Splendor' for tiferet (H8597) — the priestly/royal beauty term (Ex 28:2,40 — priestly garments made for 'glory and splendor').
textual_notes: 1 Chronicles 29:11 — 'Yours, O YHWH, is the greatness and the might and the splendor and the victory and the majesty.' The same praise vocabulary.

verses.translation: For righteous{H6664} and true{H571} is his judgment{H4941} who judged{H8199} the great{H1419} harlot{H2181} who corrupts{H7843} the earth{H776} with her fornication{H2184}, and he avenged{H5358} the blood{H1818} of his servant{H5650} from her.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַמַּשְׁחִית (hamashchit — 'who corrupts/destroys', from shachat H7843) — the SAME word as the Destroyer angel in Exodus 12:23 who struck the firstborn. The harlot IS the mashchit — the destroying agent. Greek ἔφθειρε ('corrupted') is generic. The Hebrew word identifies the harlot with the Exodus Destroyer.

Hebrew: דְּמֵי עַבְדּוֹ (demei avdo — 'the blood of his SERVANT', SINGULAR). Greek: τὸ αἷμα τῶν δούλων αὐτοῦ ('the blood of his SERVANTS', PLURAL). Singular vs. plural — Hebrew focuses on each individual servant's blood; Greek generalizes.
Hebrew order: צֶדֶק וֶאֱמֶת (tsedeq ve-emet — 'righteous AND true'). Greek order: ἀληθιναὶ καὶ δίκαιαι ('true AND righteous'). REVERSED. Hebrew puts righteousness first — Torah priority.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the blood of his servant' (singular). Greek: 'the blood of his servants' (plural).
Hebrew order: 'righteous and true.' Greek order: 'true and righteous.'
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 32:43 — 'He will avenge the blood of his servants (דם עבדיו ינקום).' The Song of Moses provides the vengeance formula.

verses.translation: And they say{H559} a second{H8145} time: HalleluYah! And the smoke{H6227} goes{H1980} from generation{H1755} to generation{H1755}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מִדּוֹר לְדוֹר (midor ledor — 'from generation to generation') — the standard OT temporal formula (Ps 33:11, 49:11, 79:13, 85:5, 89:1, 100:5, 102:12, Isa 13:20, 34:10, 51:8). Greek: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of ages'). These are COMPLETELY different temporal expressions: Hebrew uses the OT generational formula; Greek uses the Greek eternal formula. A back-translator from Greek would write לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים ('forever and ever'), NOT the OT midor ledor. This is a clear one-way marker.

This DIRECTLY quotes Isaiah 34:10 — 'its smoke shall go up from generation to generation (מדור לדור יעלה עשנה); it shall not be quenched night nor day.' Isaiah 34 describes the destruction of Edom; the Hebrew Revelation applies it to Babylon.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from generation to generation' (OT formula). Greek: 'unto the ages of ages' (Greek eternal formula). Irreconcilable temporal expressions.
textual_notes: Isaiah 34:10 — 'Its smoke shall go up from generation to generation (מדור לדור יעלה עשנה).' Verbatim source.

verses.translation: And the twenty{H6242}-four{H702} elders{H2205} and the four{H702} living creatures{H2416} fell{H5307} and prayed{H6419} to YHWH{H3068} who sits{H3427} upon the throne{H3678}, saying{H559}: Amen{H543}, HalleluYah!

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallalim — 'praying', from palal H6419) — the specific Hebrew verb for formal prayer/intercession (Gen 20:7, 1 Sam 1:10, 1 Ki 8:28-30, Dan 9:4). Greek: προσεκύνησαν ('worshipped/bowed down'). Hebrew: they PRAY (verbal communion); Greek: they WORSHIP (physical prostration). A back-translator from Greek would use השתחוו (hishtachavu — 'bowed down'), not the prayer verb.
YHWH (H3068) again vs. Greek Θεός.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'prayed' (verbal communion). Greek: 'worshipped' (physical prostration).
Hebrew: YHWH. Greek: God.

verses.translation: And one voice{H6963} went out{H3318} from the throne{H3678}: HalleluYah! Praise{H1984}, servants{H5650} of YHWH{H3068}! Praise{H1984} the name{H8034} of YHWH{H3068}! And those who fear{H3372} before him{H6440}, both small{H6996} and great{H1419}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — VERBATIM PSALM 113:1 QUOTATION: הַלְלוּיָהּ הַלְלוּ עַבְדֵי יַהְוֶה הַלְלוּ אֶת שֵׁם יַהְוֶה — this is the EXACT opening of Psalm 113, which begins the Egyptian Hallel (Ps 113-118), sung at Passover, Sukkot, and major festivals. Greek collapses this to Αἰνεῖτε τῷ Θεῷ ἡμῶν ('Praise our God') — a generic command. No back-translator from Greek's simple 'praise God' would independently reconstruct the EXACT opening of Psalm 113:1. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the chapter.
Uses YHWH THREE times in this single verse. Greek uses Θεός once. The Hebrew is saturated with the covenant name.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: full Psalm 113:1 quotation with YHWH three times. Greek: simple 'Praise our God.' The Hebrew preserves the liturgical source; the Greek reduces it.
Hebrew: 'those who fear before him.' Greek: 'those who fear him.' Hebrew adds 'before his face' (לפניו).
textual_notes: Psalm 113:1 — 'HalleluYah! Praise, servants of YHWH, praise the name of YHWH (הללויה הללו עבדי יהוה הללו את שם יהוה)!' The Egyptian Hallel opening, sung at the Passover seder.

verses.translation: And I heard{H8085} one voice{H6963}, like the voice{H6963} from a great{H1419} company and like the voice{H6963} of great{H1419} waters{H4325} and like great{H1419} thunders, saying{H559}: HalleluYah! For YHWH{H3068} has prevailed{H1396}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יַהְוֶה גָּבַר (YHWH gavar — 'YHWH has prevailed/conquered'). גָּבַר (gavar, H1396) means to be mighty, to prevail in battle, to overcome (Ex 17:11 — when Moses raised his hand, 'Israel prevailed [וגבר]'; Ps 65:3 — 'iniquities prevail [גברו] against me'; Lam 1:16 — 'the enemy has prevailed [גבר]'). Greek: ἐβασίλευσε Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Παντοκράτωρ ('the Lord God Almighty REIGNS'). COMPLETELY different: Hebrew — YHWH has WON (past tense, military victory); Greek — the Lord REIGNS (present/ongoing sovereignty). A back-translator from Greek 'reigns' would use מָלַךְ (malakh — 'reigns'), not the warrior-victory verb gavar.
Hebrew uses YHWH alone. Greek expands to 'Lord God Almighty' (Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Παντοκράτωρ) — a triple title replacing the simple Tetragrammaton.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'YHWH has prevailed' (past tense, military victory). Greek: 'the Lord God Almighty reigns' (ongoing sovereignty). Different tense, different concept.
Hebrew: YHWH (one word). Greek: 'Lord God Almighty' (three titles).
translation_notes: 'Prevailed' for gavar captures the military-victory sense — YHWH has overcome, not merely begun to rule.
textual_notes: Exodus 17:11 — 'When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed (וגבר ישראל); when he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed (וגבר עמלק).' The gavar verb is used for winning in battle.

verses.translation: Let us be glad{H8056} and give{H5414} him glory{H3519}, for the time of the wedding of the lamb{H7716} has come{H935}, and his wife{H802} is prepared.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שֶׂה (seh, H7716 — 'lamb') — the Passover lamb word, consistently throughout.

Uses אִשְׁתּוֹ (ishto — 'his wife', from ishah H802). This is the standard Hebrew word for wife/woman — not 'bride.' The lamb's companion is called his WIFE (already married), not his bride (awaiting marriage). Greek also uses γυνή ('woman/wife'). But cf. ch. 21:2 where the Hebrew uses ishah, not kalah.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'let us rejoice and be glad' (χαίρωμεν καὶ ἀγαλλιώμεθα — two verbs). Hebrew has only 'let us be glad' (one verb).
translation_notes: חֲתֻנָּה (chatunnah — 'wedding') — a post-biblical Hebrew form. No standard Strong's number.
מוּכֶנֶת (mukhenet — 'prepared/ready') — later Hebrew form. No standard Strong's number.

verses.translation: And it was given{H5414} to her to be clothed{H3847} in silk{H4897}, clean{H5355} and good{H2896} and beautiful{H3303}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses THREE qualities: נָקִי וְטוֹב וְיָפֶה (naqi vetov veyafeh — 'clean and good and beautiful'). Greek has TWO: καθαρὸν καὶ λαμπρόν ('clean and bright'). The Hebrew adds 'good' (tov) — the Genesis creation word ('and God saw that it was good'). The bride's garment has the quality of original creation.

Uses מֶשִׁי (meshi, H4897 — 'silk'). Greek: βύσσινον ('fine linen'). Different fabric. Silk is a luxury import from the East; linen is the priestly fabric (Ex 28:39). The Hebrew dresses the bride in eastern luxury; the Greek dresses her in priestly garments.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'silk' (luxury fabric). Greek: 'fine linen' (priestly fabric).
Hebrew: three qualities (clean, good, beautiful). Greek: two (clean, bright).
Greek adds: 'for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints' — an explanatory gloss absent from Hebrew.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to me: Holy{H6918} are they whom he called{H7121} to eat the evening meal{H6153} with the lamb{H7716}. And he said{H559} to me: These are the words{H1697} of YHWH{H3068} in truth{H571}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew says קְדוֹשִׁים (kedoshim — 'HOLY are they'). Greek says Μακάριοι ('BLESSED are they'). These are fundamentally different qualities: 'holy' (set apart for God) vs. 'blessed' (happy/favored). A back-translator from Greek Μακάριοι would write אַשְׁרֵי (ashrei — 'blessed/happy'), not kedoshim ('holy'). This is a clear one-way marker.

Uses אֲכִילַת עֶרֶב (akilat erev — 'the evening meal'). This echoes the PASSOVER meal, which must be eaten in the evening (Ex 12:8 — 'they shall eat the flesh that night'). Greek: τὸ δεῖπνον τοῦ γάμου ('the supper of the marriage'). Hebrew frames the meal as PASSOVER (evening meal with the lamb); Greek frames it as a WEDDING FEAST. A back-translator from Greek would write סעודת החתונה ('the wedding feast'), not 'evening meal.'
דִּבְרֵי יַהְוֶה (divrei YHWH — 'words of YHWH') vs. Greek λόγοι... τοῦ Θεοῦ ('words of God').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'holy' (kedoshim). Greek: 'blessed' (Μακάριοι). Different quality.
Hebrew: 'evening meal' (Passover context). Greek: 'marriage supper' (wedding context).
Hebrew: 'words of YHWH.' Greek: 'true words of God.'
textual_notes: Exodus 12:8 — 'And they shall eat the flesh that night (בלילה הזה), roasted with fire... with the lamb (שה).' The evening meal with the lamb is the Passover.

verses.translation: And I fell{H5307} at his feet{H7272} to pray{H6419} to him, and he said{H559} to me: See{H7200}! Do not do{H6213} so! I am your companion{H2270} and of your brothers{H251} and of those who have the testimony{H5715} of Yeshua. Make{H6213} your prayer{H8605} to YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חֲבֵרֶיךָ (chavereykhа — 'your companion/friend', from chaver H2270). Greek: σύνδουλός σου ('your fellow-servant/co-slave'). FUNDAMENTALLY different relationship: Hebrew — companion/friend (equality, friendship); Greek — fellow-slave (shared servitude). The Hebrew chaver is the rabbinic term for a study partner and friend (b. Berakhot 63b: 'acquire for yourself a chaver'). A back-translator from Greek σύνδουλος would use עבד ('servant/slave'), NEVER the friendship-based chaver.

Uses עֲשֵׂי תְּפִילָּתְךָ לְיַהְוֶה ('make your prayer to YHWH'). Greek: τῷ Θεῷ προσκύνησον ('worship God'). Hebrew: PRAY to YHWH (verbal communication); Greek: WORSHIP God (physical act). And again YHWH vs. God.
Greek adds: 'for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy' (ἡ γὰρ μαρτυρία Ἰησοῦ ἐστι τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς προφητείας) — absent from Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your companion' (friendship). Greek: 'your fellow-servant' (servitude).
Hebrew: 'make your prayer to YHWH.' Greek: 'worship God.'
Greek adds the interpretive gloss about testimony and the spirit of prophecy.
translation_notes: 'Companion' for chaver preserves the Hebrew friendship/study-partner relationship.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} the heavens{H8064} opened{H6605}, and I saw{H7200} one{H259} horse{H5483}, white{H3836}; and this one who sits{H3427} upon it, his name{H8034} was Faithful{H539} and True{H571}, and he judges{H8199} in righteousness{H6664}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: יִשְׁפּוֹט בְּצֶדֶק (yishpot betsedeq — 'judges in righteousness') — echoes Isaiah 11:4 (וְשָׁפַט בְּצֶדֶק — 'and he shall judge in righteousness'). Greek adds: καὶ πολεμεῖ ('and makes war'). The Greek adds a military dimension absent from the Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'and makes war' (καὶ πολεμεῖ) — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'his name WAS' (שמו היה — past tense). Greek: 'called' (καλούμενος — present participle).
textual_notes: Isaiah 11:4-5 — 'He shall judge the poor in righteousness (בצדק)... righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness (אמונה) the belt of his loins.' The Messianic figure judges in righteousness and is characterized by faithfulness — matching the Hebrew name 'Faithful and True.'

verses.translation: And his eyes{H5869} were like a flame{H3852} of fire{H784}, and upon his head{H7218} many crowns{H3804}, and one{H259} name{H8034} written{H3789} upon him, and no{H3808} one knows{H3045} it except he alone{H905}.

greek_deviations: Greek adds 'which no one knew except himself' (ὃ οὐδεὶς οἶδεν εἰ μὴ αὐτός). Hebrew has the same idea but phrases it differently: 'no one knows it except he alone' (שום אחד יודע אותו רק הוא לבדו).
translation_notes: כְּתָרִים (ketarim — 'crowns') — later Hebrew plural from כתר (keter — 'crown'). Greek: διαδήματα ('diadems'). Different type of crown — Hebrew keter is a royal crown; Greek diadema is a royal headband.

verses.translation: And he was clothed{H3847} in one garment upon which blood{H1818} was sprinkled{H2236}, and his name{H8034} was the Utterance{H1697} of YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses זֹרַק (zoraq — 'sprinkled', from zaraq H2236) — the specific PRIESTLY verb for hurling/sprinkling blood against the altar (Ex 24:6 — Moses 'sprinkled [ויזרק] the blood on the altar'; Lev 1:5,11, 3:2, 7:2, Num 18:17). The garment has blood RITUALLY SPRINKLED on it — this is priestly consecration imagery. Greek: βεβαμμένον ('dipped/dyed'). Hebrew: ritual sprinkling (priestly act); Greek: dipping/dyeing (textile process). A back-translator from Greek 'dipped' would use טָבוּל (tavul — 'dipped'), not the priestly zaraq.

CRITICAL: Uses דִּיבּוּר יַהְוֶה (dibbur YHWH — 'the Utterance/Word of YHWH'). Greek: Ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ ('The Word/Logos of God'). Hebrew דִּבּוּר (dibbur) specifically means 'spoken utterance/speech act' — it emphasizes the SPOKEN nature of the divine word (cf. the Ten דִּבְּרוֹת — 'Utterances/Commandments'). Greek λόγος can mean word, reason, account, logic. And again: YHWH vs. God.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sprinkled' (priestly ritual). Greek: 'dipped' (textile dyeing). Different action.
Hebrew: 'Utterance of YHWH.' Greek: 'Word of God.'
Greek: some manuscripts have περιρεραντισμένον ('sprinkled') instead of βεβαμμένον ('dipped'), suggesting awareness of the Hebrew reading.
translation_notes: 'Utterance' for dibbur rather than 'word' — preserving the spoken-speech emphasis of the Hebrew, distinguishing it from Greek logos.
The blood-sprinkled garment echoes Isaiah 63:1-3 — 'Who is this coming from Edom, with garments stained crimson?... I have trodden the winepress alone.'
textual_notes: Exodus 24:6-8 — Moses sprinkled (ויזרק) blood on the altar AND on the people, saying 'Behold the blood of the covenant.' The blood-sprinkled garment connects to the covenant ratification.

verses.translation: And all{H3605} the hosts{H6635} of the heavens{H8064} walked{H1980} after{H310} him upon white{H3836} horses{H5483}, and all{H3605} of them wearing garments of white{H3836} silk{H4897}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses צִבְאוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם (tsiv'ot hashamayim — 'the hosts of the heavens', H6635) — the OT angelic-military term from the divine title YHWH Tsevaot ('YHWH of Hosts'). Greek: τὰ στρατεύματα τὰ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ('the armies in heaven'). Hebrew uses the specific Tsevaot vocabulary; Greek uses generic military language.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'silk' (מֶשִׁי). Greek: 'fine linen' (βύσσινον). Same fabric divergence as v8.

verses.translation: And from his mouth{H6310} goes forth a sword{H2719} of two edges, to strike{H5221} with it the peoples{H5971}; and he shall lead{H5090} them with a rod{H7626} of iron{H1270}; and he shall reprove{H3198} with uprightness{H4334} the grapes{H6025} of the earth{H776} in the fierce{H2740} anger{H639} of YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הוֹכִיחַ בְּמִישׁוֹר (hokhiach bemishor — 'reprove with uprightness') — a DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 11:4 (וְהוֹכִיחַ בְּמִישׁוֹר לְעַנְוֵי אָרֶץ — 'and he shall reprove with uprightness for the meek of the earth'). The Hebrew Revelation substitutes 'grapes of the earth' (ענבי ארץ) for Isaiah's 'meek of the earth' (ענוי ארץ) — a consonantal pun where ענב (grape) and ענו (meek) differ by one letter. This wordplay exists ONLY in Hebrew. Greek πατεῖ τὴν ληνόν ('he treads the winepress') loses the Isaiah quotation entirely and replaces the judicial reproof with physical treading.

Uses חֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת (cherev pifiyyot — 'sword of two edges/mouths') — quoting Psalm 149:6 (וְחֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת בְּיָדָם — 'and a two-edged sword in their hand'). Greek: ῥομφαία ὀξεῖα ('sharp sword'). The Hebrew preserves the Psalm citation.

Uses יְנַהֵג (yenaheg — 'shall lead/drive', from nahag H5090). Greek: ποιμανεῖ ('shall shepherd'). Hebrew 'lead/drive' (used for driving flocks and chariots) is different from Greek 'shepherd.' A back-translator would use ירעה (yir'eh — 'shepherd').

Uses בַּחֲרוֹן אַף יַהְוֶה (bacharon af YHWH — 'in the fierce anger of YHWH') — a standard OT expression occurring dozens of times (Ex 32:12, Num 25:4, Deut 13:17, Josh 7:26, 2 Ki 23:26, Jer 4:8, 30:24). Greek expands to τοῦ θυμοῦ καὶ τῆς ὀργῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ Παντοκράτορος ('the fury and wrath of God Almighty').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'reprove with uprightness the grapes of the earth' (Isaiah 11:4 + grape wordplay). Greek: 'treads the winepress of the fury and wrath of God Almighty.' Completely different imagery.
Hebrew: 'fierce anger of YHWH.' Greek: 'fury and wrath of God Almighty.'
Hebrew: 'lead' (drive). Greek: 'shepherd.'
translation_notes: The ענבי/ענוי (grapes/meek) wordplay: Isaiah 11:4 has 'the meek of the earth' (ענוי ארץ). The Hebrew Revelation changes one consonant to get 'grapes of the earth' (ענבי ארץ), fusing the Messianic judgment of Isaiah 11 with the winepress image of Isaiah 63. This is a characteristically Hebrew exegetical technique.
textual_notes: Isaiah 11:4 — 'He shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked. And he shall reprove with uprightness (והוכיח במישור) for the meek of the earth (לענוי ארץ).'
Psalm 2:9 — 'You shall break them with a rod of iron (בשבט ברזל).' The iron rod quotation.

verses.translation: And one name{H8034} was written{H3789} upon his garment: thus — King{H4428} of Kings{H4428} and Lord{H113} of Lords{H113}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: name written 'upon his garment' (על בגדו). Greek: 'upon his garment AND upon his thigh' (ἐπὶ τὸ ἱμάτιον καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν μηρὸν αὐτοῦ). Greek adds 'and upon his thigh' — absent from Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'upon his thigh' (ἐπὶ τὸν μηρὸν αὐτοῦ) — absent from Hebrew.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 10:17 — 'For YHWH your God is the God of gods and the Lord of lords (אדוני האדנים).' Daniel 2:47 — 'Your God is the God of gods and the Lord of kings (מארא מלכין).'

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} one{H259} messenger{H4397} standing{H5975} in the sun{H8121}, and he cried out{H6817} with a great{H1419} voice{H6963} and said{H559} to all{H3605} the fowl{H5775} that are under the heavens{H8064}: Go{H1980}! Gather{H622}, all of you, to the evening meal of the great Elohai{H430}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמַיִם ('under the heavens') — standard OT spatial description (Gen 1:9, 6:17, 7:19, Deut 2:25, 4:19, 25:19, 29:20). Greek: ἐν μεσουρανήματι ('in mid-heaven'). Hebrew: below the sky; Greek: in the middle of the sky. Different positions.
Again uses אֲכִילַת עֶרֶב ('evening meal') — the Passover evening meal framing, as in v9.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'under the heavens.' Greek: 'in mid-heaven.'
Hebrew: 'evening meal' (Passover context). Greek: 'supper' (δεῖπνον).
textual_notes: Ezekiel 39:17 — 'Speak to every sort of bird and to every beast of the field: Assemble and come, gather from all sides to my sacrificial feast (זבחי).' The great carrion feast of Ezekiel 39.

verses.translation: So that you may eat{H398} the flesh{H1320} of kings{H4428} and princes{H8269}, and the flesh{H1320} of mighty men{H1368}, and the flesh{H1320} of horses{H5483} and of those who ride{H7392} upon them, and the flesh{H1320} of small{H6996} and great{H1419}, and of slaves{H5650} and freemen.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גִּבּוֹרִים (gibborim — 'mighty men', H1368) — the OT warrior elite: the gibborim of Genesis 6:4 ('the mighty men of old'), David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:8ff, 1 Chr 11:10ff). Greek: ἰσχυρῶν ('strong men'). The Hebrew carries the weight of the biblical warrior tradition.

Uses מְשׁוּחְרָרִים (meshuchrarim — 'freemen/emancipated ones') — a specifically LEGAL later Hebrew term for manumitted slaves, from the root שחרר. Greek: ἐλευθέρων ('free persons'). The Hebrew implies freed slaves; the Greek implies freeborn citizens.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'princes' (שרים — governmental officials). Greek: 'captains of thousands' (χιλιάρχων — specific military rank).
textual_notes: Ezekiel 39:18-20 — 'You shall eat the flesh of the mighty (גבורים) and drink the blood of the princes (נשיאי) of the earth.' The Ezekiel 39 carrion feast provides the vocabulary.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} the beast{H2416} and the kings{H4428} of the earth{H776} who gathered{H622} their encampments{H4264} to make{H6213} war{H4421} with the one who sits{H3427} upon [...] the horse{H5483} and with his encampment{H4264}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַחֲנֵיהֶם (machaneihem — 'their encampments', from machaneh H4264) — the specific OT military camp word (Gen 32:2 — Jacob's 'two camps'; Ex 14:19-20 — the camp of Israel; Num 2 — the arrangement of Israel's camp). Greek: τὰ στρατεύματα ('the armies'). Hebrew uses the OT tribal-military encampment concept; Greek uses a generic army term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew has a lacuna [...] before 'the horse,' suggesting a missing word in the manuscript.

verses.translation: And the beast{H2416} was captured{H7617}, with the prophet{H5030} of the falsehood{H8267} who did{H6213} the signs{H226} before it — to lead astray{H5496} those who took the mark of the beast{H2416} [...] and who prayed{H6419} to it — and they were cast{H7993} into the Sheol{H7585} that burns{H1197} with sulfur{H1614}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נְבִיא הַשֶּׁקֶר (nevi hasheqer — 'the prophet of THE FALSEHOOD', H5030 + H8267). This is the EXACT OT construction from Jeremiah: נְבִיאֵי שֶׁקֶר ('prophets of falsehood' — Jer 23:25-26, 27:15, 29:9). Greek ψευδοπροφήτης ('false prophet') is a Greek compound word. The Hebrew preserves Jeremiah's construction with the definite article (the falsehood — a specific entity); the Greek creates a new compound word.

CRITICAL: Uses בִּשְׁאוֹל הַבּוֹעֵר בְּגָפְרִית ('into the Sheol that burns with sulfur'). Greek: εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρός ('into the lake of fire'). AGAIN: Hebrew has SHEOL (the underworld); Greek has 'lake of fire.' This is the SAME consistent pattern seen in ch. 17:8,11, 20:10, and 21:8. The Hebrew ALWAYS uses Sheol where the Greek has 'lake of fire.' This is perhaps the most persistent one-way marker in all of Revelation.

Uses לְהַסִּית (lehasit — 'to lead astray/incite', from sut H5496) — the specific Torah verb for inciting to idolatry (Deut 13:6 — 'if your brother incites you [יסיתך] to serve other gods'). Greek: ἐπλάνησε ('deceived').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Sheol that burns with sulfur.' Greek: 'lake of fire burning with sulfur.' Sheol vs. lake of fire.
Hebrew: 'prophet of the falsehood' (Jeremiah construction). Greek: 'false prophet' (compound word).
Greek adds 'alive' (ζῶντες) and 'the two' (οἱ δύο) — absent from Hebrew.
Greek adds 'those who worshipped its image' (τοὺς προσκυνοῦντας τῇ εἰκόνι αὐτοῦ). Hebrew has only 'who prayed to it' — without 'image.'
translation_notes: סִימָן (siman — 'mark/sign') — later Hebrew term. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Genesis 19:24 — 'YHWH rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire (גפרית ואש).' The burning sulfur connects to the paradigmatic divine judgment.

verses.translation: And the rest were slain{H2026} by{H3027} the sword{H2719} from the one who sits{H3427} upon the horse{H5483}, which went forth{H3318} from his mouth{H6310}; and all{H3605} the beasts{H2416} of the field{H7704} were sated{H7646} from their flesh{H1320}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חַיּוֹת הַשָּׂדֶה (chayyot hasadeh — 'beasts of the field', H2416 + H7704) — the standard OT phrase for wild animals (Gen 2:19-20, 3:1,14, 1 Sam 17:44,46, Ezek 34:5,8, 39:4,17). Greek: πάντα τὰ ὄρνεα ('all the birds'). Hebrew: BEASTS OF THE FIELD eat the flesh; Greek: BIRDS eat the flesh. Completely different animals. A back-translator from Greek 'birds' would write עופות (ofot — 'birds'), not chayyot hasadeh. The Hebrew preserves the Ezekiel 39 terminology where both beasts and birds feast on the fallen.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'beasts of the field' (wild animals). Greek: 'all the birds.' Different animals.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 39:4 — 'I will give you to the birds of prey and to the beasts of the field (חית השדה) to be devoured.' Ezekiel 39:17 — 'Speak to every bird and every beast of the field: Assemble and come.' The Hebrew Revelation uses the Ezekiel phrase.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 19 in Hebrew is dominated by Hallel liturgy and Isaiah quotations. The most striking one-way markers are: (1) The VERBATIM Psalm 113:1 quotation (הללו עבדי יהוה הללו את שם יהוה) where Greek collapses it to a generic 'praise God'; (2) YHWH גָּבַר ('YHWH has prevailed/conquered') vs. Greek 'the Lord God Almighty reigns' — military victory vs. ongoing sovereignty; (3) מִדּוֹר לְדוֹר ('from generation to generation') vs. Greek 'forever and ever' — OT temporal formula vs. Greek eternal formula, directly from Isaiah 34:10; (4) The priestly blood-SPRINKLING verb זרק (zaraq) vs. Greek 'dipped'; (5) דִּיבּוּר יהוה ('Utterance of YHWH') vs. 'Logos of God'; (6) The Isaiah 11:4 quote הוכיח במישור with the ענבי/ענוי (grapes/meek) consonantal pun; (7) חבר ('companion') vs. Greek 'fellow-slave'; (8) קדושים ('holy') vs. Greek 'blessed' for the wedding-feast guests; (9) Sheol vs. 'lake of fire' (consistent pattern); and (10) חיות השדה ('beasts of the field') vs. Greek 'birds.' The chapter's HalleluYah-saturated worship sections demonstrate organic Hebrew liturgical composition.
